text:
December pay lands early, and then January feels like it lasts forever. Last festive season South Africans planned to spend more than R289 billion (Wonga survey), and in January almost six in ten said they were worse off (Debt Rescue). Here's how to plan January before you spend December, with real numbers: Lindiwe (an illustration) takes home R14,000, gets her December pay on 15 December and her next pay on 29 January, 45 days later. We list everything due before then, pay January first, set her festive budget from what's left (plus her stokvel payout), keep a cushion, and give every rand a job. Then the four traps (credit, quick loans, the bonus and social pressure), what to do if January is already tight, and how to start saving for next December now.

Key facts
- Wonga Summer Spending Survey (10,000+ people, Dec 2025): planned festive spend of more than R289 billion; average R6,299 a person (food and drinks R2,261, travel and transport R1,166, gifts R1,135); 22% planned to use credit; 23% saved through the year; money was the gift most people wanted (49%).
- Debt Rescue (Jan 2026): 58.5% financially worse off after the festive season; 37% named back-to-school costs as their biggest expense and worry.
- Standard Bank (Dec 2024): after a mid-December payday, 42 days to the next pay for people usually paid on the 25th and 49 days for month-end earners.
- Public schools open on 13 January 2027.
- Brand Journal (Nov 2026): December 2025 retail sales about 45% above an average month earlier in the year.
- National Credit Regulator: borrow only from registered credit providers, and don't let social pressure get you into debt.

About the example: Lindiwe is an illustration. Paid 15 Dec 2026, next pay 29 Jan 2027 = 45 days. Due before then: rent R4,000 + debit orders R900 + taxi fare R2,400 + groceries R4,500 + back to school R1,200 = R13,000; left from R14,000: R1,000; plus a R6,000 stokvel payout = R7,000; R1,000 cushion; R6,000 to spend. R500 a month from January to December = R6,000.
